paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most homes contain a number of objects that are used only rarely. An electric drill may come out of the cupboard to put up a single shelf and then not be touched again for a year. A ladder is needed once a season to clear the gutters, and a large cooking pot appears only when relatives visit. Each of these objects had to be bought, carried home and stored, and each takes up space that could be used for something else. In recent decades, groups of neighbours in a number of countries have asked a simple question: if an object is needed so seldom, why should every household own one? Their answer has been the 'library of things', a lending service for objects rather than books.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The basic idea is borrowed directly from the public library. Members join, browse a catalogue and take an item home for a fixed period, usually a few days or a week. When they return it, the next person can use it. The catalogue of a typical library of things is wide. Alongside drills and ladders, it may include sewing machines, tents, camping stoves, carpet cleaners, projectors, board games and musical instruments. Some libraries specialise: one might focus on garden equipment, while another lends mainly kitchen appliances for people who wish to try a new style of cooking before spending money on it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Most libraries of things begin as small volunteer projects. A few enthusiastic residents collect unwanted items from friends and neighbours, find a free corner in a community centre or a church hall, and open for a few hours each weekend. Donations are the main source of stock, which means that the early collection often reflects what people happened to have in their garages rather than what borrowers actually need. Over time, the more successful libraries begin to keep records of which items are borrowed most often, and they use any money they receive to buy more of those.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Money is a constant concern. Some libraries charge an annual membership fee, others ask for a small payment each time an item is borrowed, and a few rely entirely on grants and gifts. Each model has drawbacks. A membership fee can discourage people who only want to try the service once, while a charge for each loan requires someone to handle payments and keep accounts. Many organisers say that the fee matters less than the location: a library that is difficult to reach by public transport will struggle to attract members whatever it charges.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Lending objects also creates problems that a book library rarely faces. A drill can be returned with a broken part, a tent can come back wet and begin to grow mould, and a sewing machine may need adjusting after every few loans. For this reason, many libraries check each item when it is returned, and some ask borrowers to sign an agreement accepting responsibility for damage. Volunteers who are skilled at repairs are especially valued. In several places, the library of things has joined forces with a repair group, so that broken items can be fixed rather than thrown away.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Supporters argue that the benefits go beyond saving money. Fewer purchases mean that fewer goods have to be manufactured and transported, and fewer end up in landfill. Libraries of things also bring together people who might not otherwise meet: a retired carpenter explaining to a young family how to use a saw safely is a common scene. Critics reply that the effect on overall consumption is difficult to measure, and that people who borrow a tool may simply buy one later. Even so, many members say that the experience has changed the way they think about ownership, and that they now ask whether they really need an object before buying it.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of human history, salt was far more valuable than it is today. Before refrigeration, it was one of the few reliable ways of preserving meat and fish, and communities without a local supply had to trade for it, sometimes over great distances. Salt could be dug from underground deposits, boiled out of the water from salt springs, or collected from the sea. The last of these methods, which relies largely on the sun and the wind, is still practised along many coastlines, and in some places it has changed surprisingly little over the centuries.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The principle behind sea salt production is simple. Seawater contains dissolved salt; if the water is removed, the salt remains. A traditional salt works makes use of this by guiding seawater through a series of shallow ponds. In the first ponds, the water is deep enough that little happens except slow evaporation. As it moves from one pond to the next, it becomes steadily more concentrated, and other minerals that are less soluble than salt begin to settle out. By the time the water reaches the final ponds, known as crystallising pans, it is so saturated that salt crystals begin to form on the surface and on the floor of the pan.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not every coastline is suitable. A salt works needs flat land close to sea level, so that water can be let in at high tide and moved between ponds with little pumping. The ground must hold water rather than allowing it to drain away, which is why clay soils are preferred. Above all, the climate must be right. Long periods of sunshine and steady, dry winds speed up evaporation, while a humid climate slows it down. For this reason, salt making by the sun has traditionally been concentrated in regions with hot, dry summers.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The harvest itself is demanding work. When a layer of crystals has formed on the floor of a crystallising pan, workers draw it together with long wooden rakes, taking care not to scrape up the clay beneath, which would discolour the salt. The salt is then piled into heaps beside the pans to drain and dry. In some regions, a thin crust of delicate crystals that forms on the surface of the water is skimmed off separately by hand. Because this surface salt is produced in small quantities and requires careful work, it is usually sold at a much higher price than ordinary sea salt.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Weather is the salt maker's greatest risk. A single heavy shower can dilute the brine in the crystallising pans and undo weeks of evaporation, and a cool, cloudy summer may produce only a small part of a normal harvest. Salt workers have therefore always watched the sky closely. In the past, much of this knowledge was passed down within families; today it is often combined with detailed forecasts, but many workers still say that experience is the best guide to when the brine is ready.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In the twentieth century, many small salt works closed. Industrial producers could obtain salt more cheaply, either by mining it or by evaporating brine in heated vessels, and the land occupied by the ponds was often more valuable for housing, tourism or ports. In recent years, however, some traditional sites have found new life. Interest in local food has created a market for hand-harvested salt, and abandoned ponds have been restored, partly for production and partly because the shallow water provides feeding grounds for wading birds. Several salt works now welcome visitors, who can watch the harvest and learn how a centuries-old technique still works.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: No language exists in isolation. Wherever speakers of different languages trade, travel, marry or go to war with one another, words pass between them. Linguists call these words loanwords, although the term is misleading: nothing is ever given back, and the language that lends a word loses nothing by doing so. English is often described as a heavy borrower, having taken large parts of its vocabulary from French and Latin, but it is far from unusual. Uzbek, for example, contains many words of Arabic and Persian origin, as well as a more recent layer borrowed from Russian and, increasingly, from English.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most obvious reason for borrowing is need. When a community encounters a new object, plant, animal or idea, it may simply adopt the name used by the people who introduced it. Words for foods and drinks often travel this way, along with the goods themselves; the names for tea and coffee, for instance, have spread across many languages in recognisably similar forms. Technical vocabulary follows the same pattern. A language whose speakers adopt a new technology from abroad will frequently adopt its terminology too, at least at first.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Need, however, cannot explain all borrowing. Languages regularly take in words for which they already have perfectly good equivalents. In such cases the motive is usually prestige. If one group is wealthier, more powerful or more fashionable than another, its language tends to be seen as more sophisticated, and words taken from it carry a certain status. A speaker who uses the borrowed word may be signalling education, modernity or membership of a particular social group. Over time, the native word and the loanword may both survive, but with a difference in tone or meaning. English, for example, kept the native word 'cow' for the animal but adopted 'beef', from French, for its meat.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Once a word has been borrowed, it rarely stays exactly as it was. Speakers tend to pronounce it using the sounds of their own language, so that a sound which does not exist in the borrowing language is replaced by the nearest available one. The word may also be fitted into the grammar of its new home, taking local endings for the plural or for different verb forms. After several generations, a loanword can become so thoroughly adapted that ordinary speakers no longer recognise it as foreign at all, and only a dictionary that records word histories will reveal where it came from.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Borrowing does not always involve taking the foreign word itself. Sometimes a language copies the structure of a foreign expression while using its own words, a process known as calquing or loan translation. The English word 'skyscraper', for example, has been translated part by part into a number of European languages, producing words that mean, literally, something like 'cloud-scraper' or 'sky-scratcher'. Because calques are built from native material, they are often harder to identify than ordinary loanwords, and speakers may be entirely unaware that an expression they use every day was modelled on another language.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone welcomes borrowing. In many countries, there have been movements to limit the number of foreign words in the national language, sometimes supported by official bodies that propose native alternatives for new technical terms. Supporters of such efforts argue that heavy borrowing makes a language harder for older or less educated speakers to understand and weakens its ability to create words of its own. The results have been mixed. Some proposed native terms have been widely adopted, while others are used mainly in official documents and are ignored in everyday speech.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Many linguists are sceptical of the idea that borrowing threatens a language. They point out that the basic vocabulary of a language, such as its words for body parts, close family members and common actions, tends to resist replacement far more strongly than vocabulary for specialised or fashionable things. A language can absorb thousands of loanwords and remain recognisably itself, because its grammar and its most frequently used words continue to be passed from parents to children. From this perspective, borrowing is less a sign of weakness than evidence of contact, and the history of a language's loanwords can be read as a record of the people its speakers have met.
